lectures.title: Autoremoving Old Dependencies to Maintain a Lean System

cues.en: Let's now have a look at how we can auto remove packages.
Why would we want to do it?
Well, full upgrade or dist upgrade only uninstalls dependencies if they are exclusive and they need
to be uninstalled in order to perform an upgrade.
So when a dependency, for example, if a package that we want to upgrade no longer needs a dependency,
but this having that dependency on our system doesn't hurt our system and doesn't hurt our upgrade procedure,
then it won't be uninstalled.
So it may leave dependencies behind that are no longer needed and that we need to uninstall manually.
So we want to uninstall them.
So in order to do that we can use auto remove, I mean apt auto remove or apt get auto remove to automatically
remove those those dependencies.
Let's have a look at that here.
So I can say sudo apt auto remove and then I hit enter and then I need to enter my password again here.
But you can see here those are the packages that it wants to remove because they are no longer needed.
And here it's 109MB of disk space.
It's not that much about the disk space.
It's more about also about potential security risks.
For example, if there was a bug in that software, well, if it's uninstalled, the bug doesn't affect
us anymore.
So this is why we should every now and then run this auto remove, especially after larger updates.
So here in this case, I just hit enter to continue that and now we see a few software packages or a
few libraries have been deleted because we no longer need them.
So this is the auto remove command and you should run this every now and then.
Now, you know pretty much everything you need in order to keep your system up to date.
And also you can install additional packages and all of that.
But now we see it gets a bit more complicated.
In the next lectures.
We want to have a look at how you can add additional repositories.
For example, you want a newer version of PHP than what's available on Ubuntu or a newer version of
node.
Or you want um, specific additional software that's not available through the default repositories.
So in the next lecture we will have a look at the repositories file.
What's the file format there?
How, how is this structured?
And then we will have a look at how you can add custom repositories and what's the risk associated with
that.
But that's the topic for the next lecture.
See you in the next video.
